 Search The Site 3 Things To Remember Now That We’re Officially Into The Darkest Part Of The Year With Earlier Sunsets And Less Daylight 3 Things To Remember Now That We’re Officially Into The Darkest Part Of The Year With Earlier Sunsets And Less Daylight
 Cori Cori Published: November 20, 2026 Photo by Alex Kalinin on Unsplash Share on Facebook 
 Share on Twitter 
 We're a couple of weeks out from the end of Daylight Saving Time, which wrapped up on November 1st this year. With that time change comes another change, a decrease in the number of daylight hours we're used to.
 Photo by Chandler Lane on Unsplash A truck driving down a road at night According to the Almanac , we've officially entered the "darkest" part of the year.
 "Daylight drops fastest around the equinoxes and slows down as the winter solstice approaches."
 vit-plus vit-plus Get our free mobile app The sun now sets earlier, and conditions stay dark longer. This has an impact on safety across the state, especially as it pertains to driving. Visibility becomes much more of an issue.
 Read More: Broadway In Bangor Closed Friday Morning After Accident 
 And there are 3 factors you may want to keep in mind when it comes to safety in those darker hours; animals, delivery drivers and kids.
 1.) Animals 
 Unaware of our implemented time changes, many animals use the cover of darkness to move from place to place.
 Photo by Gelu Iancu on Unsplash a couple of deer standing on top of a grass covered field Scanning the roadways for shadows or eye reflections, along with making sure you're alert are steps you can take to lessen your chance of colliding with an animal, big or small.
 Pascal-L-Marius Pascal-L-Marius Aside from the morning commute, them majority of motorists are on the road between the hours of  3PM and 6PM. Taking extra care to stay aware of your surroundings as the sun goes down is key.
 2.) Delivery Drivers 
 While you may not have thought anything of leaving your porch light or front door light off during the day before, it's important to consider that a number of your friendly, neighborhood delivery drivers work well into the evening, sometimes till 8 or 9 PM
 Photo by Adhitya Sibikumar on Unsplash A stack of red boxes sitting on top of a table If the sun goes down around 4 PM, and you don't get home from work till after 5 PM, there's a good chance whomever is brining that package to your house will be coming up an unlit driveway or stairwell.
 hikesterson hikesterson Do your delivery person a solid and turn your outside lights on earlier.  Light up your house for safety, not just the holidays!
 And it's not just the UPS, FedEX or mail carriers you should consider, but those that deliver propane, oil and even doordashers.
 Have their back, by lighting their way.
 3.) Kids 
 After a long day in school, many kids head home to play.
 Photo by Daniil Silantev on Unsplash Boy watching the sunset over a field Whether on their walk or bike back to the house, or their attempt to meet up with friends in their neighborhoods, it's likely that by the time they start their journeys for the afternoon, darkness will be setting in.
 And sense safety isn't always front-and-center on the mind of a child, it should be in your mind.
 BobMcLeanLLC Children at Play Sign Diamond Shaped Making sure your kids know to wear something light colored or even reflective is so important. Talking with your kids about staying out of the shadows, and near streetlights while they're moving from place to place is another things you can do to help keep kids safe.
 Read More: Show Us Bangor + Eastern Maine Holiday Light Displays 
 Most important of all, in my opinion, would be to communicate to them that it's not only their own surrounding in space that they should be aware of, but where things like cars and cyclists are in the roadway.
 PinkBadger car in blurred motion in city street with switched on headlights in autumn It's also a good thing for drivers to approach any school bus, school zone, crosswalk or and residential sidestreet slowly and with caution this time of year after sunset.
 Photo by Alex Kalinin on Unsplash Sunset over a road between dark trees The good news is the darkness doesn't last forever. There is light at the end of the tunnel, which we can wait out to enjoy, if we keep in mind these ways to keep ourselves and others safe this season.
 Good luck!
